title: One Year Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
summary:
The Commerce Department is pausing for one year a recent rule that would have automatically extended U.S. export restrictions to the affiliates of companies already on the government’s export restrictions list. The pause starts November 10, 2025, and the department says the rule is set to snap back into place on November 10, 2026, unless it decides otherwise. In a separate move, the government also removed one company in China and several related names from the restrictions list after reviewing new information and compliance commitments.

What’s being paused is a rule from late September that treated any company at least half-owned by a listed entity as if it were listed too, even if it wasn’t named. For the next year, those automatic affiliate restrictions will not apply, while the government reassesses the national security and foreign policy impacts. The department has already laid out that the same restrictions will return in November 2026, creating a clear timeline for businesses to plan around.

Who stands to benefit during the pause? U.S. and international companies that do business with non-listed affiliates of listed firms will face fewer licensing hurdles for a year, which could mean faster shipments and fewer deal delays. Exporters and compliance teams may see a small but real paperwork break; the government estimates roughly 245 fewer license applications during the pause. The company and aliases removed from the list also gain new access to U.S. goods and partners, provided they uphold their compliance promises.

Who could be negatively affected? Security-focused stakeholders may worry that easing restrictions on affiliates could create room for evasive behavior, even if only temporarily. Companies that already invested to comply with the now-paused rule may feel whiplash and face added costs adjusting twice—now and again when the rule returns. The planned snapback in November 2026 also introduces timing risk: contracts and supply chains that rely on the pause may need to revert quickly, which could disrupt operations or require fresh licenses.

The bottom line: this is a time-limited reset, not a rollback. Businesses get a year of breathing room and a chance to fine-tune compliance, but they should prepare for the restrictions to return on November 10, 2026. Meanwhile, the selective removal of one company and several aliases from the list shows that the government is still willing to adjust based on new facts and stronger compliance safeguards.
